newsitem.title: USA: Scant impact seen on U.S. CPI from Florida freeze.
newsitem.headline: Scant impact seen on U.S. CPI from Florida freeze.

text.p: A cold snap that damaged fruit and vegetable crops in Florida last weekend is unlikely to have a major impact on the overall Consumer Price Index, a Labor Department economist said Friday.
"Certainly the bigger impact could be on the February CPI rather than January," said Patrick Jackman, economist with the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics, which issues the CPI.

While supermarkets in the eastern and midwestern states have already marked up some prices to account for diminished produce supply, Jackman said given the timing of when the CPI data are collected, most of the effects would not show up until the February survey.

However, he said that even if the damage results in large increases in supermarket prices, the effect on the CPI is likely to be small as the affected produce makes up only a small portion of the overall index.

"Total fresh fruits and vegetables make up about 1.3 percent of the CPI," Jackman said, adding that citrus fruits, the primary area of concern, are just one part of the total fruits and vegetables included in the price survey.
To have boost the monthly CPI by even a few tenths of a percentage point would require a huge spike in fruit and vegetable prices.

Even then, Jackman said the impact would be mitigated by seasonal adjustment factors, which expect some degree of price rises in the winter months resulting from cold spells in various parts of the country.

Temperatures in Florida last weekend fell as low as 19 degrees Farenheit in the worst cold spell to hit the fruit and vegetable industry since December 1989. Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles said the statewide losses for the crops could top $270 million.
The Labor Department is scheduled to issue its report on consumer prices for January on Feb. 19.
